## Personality

Harried, honest and allergic to shortcuts. He carries a set of weights and checks everyone's scales.

## Lore

Reynold is forty-seven, the Warden of the Crown Market, and he is always slightly out of breath. The Crown Market is the busiest place on Veligor, and keeping order in it is a job for three men, so Reynold does the work of three, at a fast walk, with a frown and a heavy leather case under his arm. In the case is a set of brass weights, from a pound down to a quarter-ounce, each one stamped and checked against the palace standard. He uses them on everyone's scales. Everyone's. He is harried, honest to the bone and allergic to shortcuts, and the stallholders say, half in complaint and half in pride, that there is no market on the island with fairer weight.

### The warden's round

He took the post eleven years ago, when the old warden retired, and he walks the market from the opening bell to the last lamp. He settles squabbles over stall space, which are endless, and over whose awning drips on whose cheeses, which are worse. He checks scales, measures and yardsticks, chases off sellers of cracked pots and watered milk, and keeps a ledger of every complaint and how it was settled, so that when the same two stallholders come to him for the ninth time he can tell them what he decided the previous eight. He has no power to fine anyone very much. He relies instead on the fact that a stall Reynold has called short-weight in front of its customers does not do much trade for a week.

He grew up in the back streets behind the market, the son of a porter. His mother sold dried peas and beans by the scoop, and when he was nine he watched a dishonest weigher cheat her out of a winter's earnings with a doctored scale, and watched her say nothing because she could not prove it. Both his parents are dead now. He has never forgotten the scale. He has never married, either. He says he would have to check her scales and it would start them off badly.

### Wat

Two summers ago a thin, fast boy of nine tried for Reynold's own purse in the middle of the cloth row. Reynold caught his wrist without looking round. He had noticed the boy about the market more than once that year, too quick and too thin and never buying anything, and had half suspected, without ever catching him at it. Instead of marching him to the Guard, Reynold asked him how fast he could get a message to the far end of the market. The boy told him. Reynold timed him, and gave him a job.

That boy is Wat, who is eleven now and runs Reynold's errands: messages, measures, warnings about short weights, summonses to stallholders who are about to have a very bad afternoon. The evening he hired him, Reynold walked Wat up to Selene's forge and told his elder brother Kenric everything, because he would not keep a boy's secret from the person responsible for him. Kenric thanked him three times. Reynold found it very difficult to know what to do with that, and went home and checked his weights.

Wat now tells strangers when their purses are badly tied. Reynold has never told him how proud that makes him. He suspects Wat knows.

### What the market is saying

Lately the market is quieter in a way Reynold does not like. Carts come in late or in convoys. Prices on goods from the far towns have jumped, not from greed, as he first suspected and checked, but from the cost of guards on the road. More stalls sell blades and potions than did five years ago, and fewer sell lace.

### What he wants and fears

Reynold wants a market where every scale is true and every quarrel is settled before sundown. What he fears is someone from Wat's old days turning up in the market, and having to choose between the rules and the boy.

A quest might begin with a set of weights that read true on Reynold's scale and false on everyone else's, or with Wat failing to come back from an errand to the far end of the market.
